title: Kannappa, who gave his eye
hookLine: a hunter who didn't know the rules offers Shiva everything, including his own eye
carry: Shiva receives love before the rules
tomorrow: a princess says she's already married. to Krishna.

lines: A PRIEST AND HIS PERFECT RITUAL.
cards: A temple priest in the hills of the south arrives each morning to do the worship properly: the water, the flowers, the mantras, all in order. And every morning he finds the shrine a mess. Meat on the floor.
Water splashed everywhere. Wilted wildflowers. Someone is getting in overnight and defiling it.
He's heartbroken. So one night he hides, to catch whoever's doing it. What he sees, the story says, turns his idea of proper worship upside down.

teach.b: The Nayanars are the Alvars' neighbors: sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva. The poet Sekkizhar gathered their stories in the Periya Puranam, the great story.
Three of them, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, left hymns, the Tevaram, still sung in Shiva temples. And one of them is the hunter the priest saw that night. His name was Thinnan.
He'd found the Shiva linga in the forest and fallen completely in love.

teach.h: A HUNTER WHO KNEW NO RULES.
teach.b: He knew none of the rules, so he worshiped the way a hunter would. He carried water in his own mouth and poured it over the linga. He brought flowers tucked in his hair.
He offered the best meat from his hunt, tasted first to make sure it was good. The priest watched, horrified. Then, the story says, one of the eyes on the linga began to bleed.
Thinnan didn't hesitate. He cut out his own eye and pressed it into place. The bleeding stopped.
Then the other eye began to bleed. He had one eye left, and he'd need to find the spot once he was blind, so he put his foot on the linga to mark it and raised the arrow. And Shiva stopped his hand.
From that day he's been called Kannappa, the one who gave his eye.
The Nayanars also include a woman poet, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, whom Shiva, the story says, called mother, and a laborer, Nandanar, kept outside the temple, who longed only to see Shiva dance.

teach.h: SHIVA RECEIVES LOVE BEFORE THE RULES.
teach.b: That's the Nayanars' teaching: Shiva receives love before the rules. Shiva temples still keep the rituals; many teachers read the story as showing what the rituals are for.

how: In Tamil Shaiva temples, hymns of the Nayanars (the Tevaram and others) are sung in temple worship, images of the sixty-three saints often line the temple halls, and the Periya Puranam's stories, like Kannappa's, are retold at festivals and to children.

o: a rule that only priests may touch a temple image
love for God that can come before knowing any rules
a vow to give up hunting and eating meat for life

s: Kannappa learned the proper rituals before worshiping Shiva

games.q: you're Kannappa. you've given one eye to stop the linga's bleeding. now the other eye bleeds, and you'll be blind. what do you do?
o: mark the spot with your foot and reach for the arrow.
games.why: he marks the spot with his foot so he can find it blind, and raises the arrow. Shiva stops his hand.

practice: Think of the way you show love when nobody's grading you: clumsy, maybe too much, cooking, fixing things, showing up with the wrong flowers. See it without embarrassment, and let it be enough.
If you pray, offer your own clumsy way of loving, the hunter's way, just as it is; if not, rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti yoga, through the Nayanars: sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva. Kannappa the hunter, who gave his eye, shows love that comes before the rules.

orig.note: Tamil: nayanmar, the Nayanars, 'leaders' or 'masters'; the sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: Shiva receives love before the rules. He took the hunter's clumsy love just as it came. See you tomorrow.
